The '''Liburnian language''', spoken by the [[Liburnians]] in classical times, is reckoned as an [[Indo-European language]] with a significant proportion of the [[Pre-Indo-European languages|Pre-Indo-European]] elements from the wider area of the ancient [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]], but is basically unattested and unclassified. Due to the paucity of evidence, the very existence of a distinct 'Liburnian language' must be considered hypothetical at this point.

==Classification==
No writings in Liburnian are known. The only presumed Liburnian linguistic remains are Liburnian toponyms and some family and personal names in [[Liburnia]] presumed to be native to the area, in Latinized form from the 1st century AD. Smaller differences found in the archaeological material of narrower regions in Liburnia are in a certain measure reflected also in these scarce linguistic remains. This has caused much speculation about the language but no certainty.

Features shared by Liburnian and other languages have been noted in Liburnian language remains, names and toponyms, dating from between the [[Iron Age]] and the beginning of the [[Common Era]]. These are insufficient for a precise linguistic classification, other than a general indication that they have an Indo-European basis, but also may incorporate significant elements from Pre-Indo-European languages. This also appears to be the case in their social relations, and such phenomena are likely related to their separate cultural development, physical isolation and mixed ethnic origins.<ref>D. Rendić-Miočević, ''Onomastičke studije s područja Liburna,'' Zbornik Instituta za historijske nauke u Zadru 1, 1955</ref><ref>M. Suić, ''Zapadne granice Ilira u svijetlu historijskih izvora,'' Simpozijum, 1966</ref>{{sfn|Batović|2005|p=65, 66}}

Following studies of the onomastics of the [[Dalmatia (Roman province)|Roman province of Dalmatia]], [[Géza Alföldy]] has suggested that the Liburni and [[Histri]] belonged to the [[Venetic language]] area.{{sfn|Alföldy|1964}}{{sfn|Alföldy|1969}} In particular, some Liburnian [[anthroponyms]] show strong Venetic affinities, a few similar names and common roots, such as ''Vols-'', ''Volt-'', and ''Host-'' (< [[PIE]] ''*ghos-ti-'' 'stranger, guest, host'). Liburnian and Venetic names sometimes also share suffixes in common, such as ''-icus'' and ''-ocus''.

[[Jürgen Untermann]], who has focused on Liburnian and Venetic onomastics, considers that only the Liburnians at the north-eastern [[Istria]]n coast were strongly Venetic. Untermann has suggested three groups of Liburnian names: one structurally similar to those of the Veneti and Histri; another linked to the [[Dalmatae]], [[Iapodes]] and other [[Illyrians]] on the mainland to the south of the Liburnians, and a third group of names that were common throughout Liburnian territory, and lacked any relation to those of their neighbors.<ref>J. Untermann, ''Die venetischen Personennamen,'' Wiesbaden, 1961</ref><ref>J. Untermann, ''Venetisches in Dalmatien,'' GCBI 5, 1970</ref>

Other proper names, such as those of local deities and toponyms also showed differing regional distributions. According to [[Radoslav Katičić|R. Katičić]], Liburnian toponyms, in both structure and form, demonstrate diverse influences, including [[Old European hydronymy|Pre-Indo-European]], Indo-European and other, purely local features. Katičić has also stated that toponyms were distributed separately along ethnic and linguistic lines.{{sfn|Katicic|1976|p={{page needed|date=February 2025}}}}

S. Čače has noted that it can not be determined whether Liburnian was more related to the North Adriatic language group (Veneti, Histri) or the languages of Iapodes and Dalmatae, due to the scarcity of evidence.<ref>S. Čače, Liburnija u razdoblju od 4. do 1. st. prije nove ere, Zadar, 1985, 101-120</ref> While the Liburnians differed significantly from the Histri and Veneti, both culturally and ethnically, they have been linked to the Dalmatae by their burial traditions. 

Other toponymical and onomastic similarities have been found between Liburnia and other regions of both Illyria and [[Asia Minor]], especially [[Lycia]], [[Lydia]], [[Caria]], [[Pisidia]], [[Isauria]], [[Pamphylia]], [[Lycaonia]] and [[Cilicia]], as well as similarities in elements of social organization, such as [[matriarchy]]/[[Gynocentrism|gynecocracy]] (''gynaikokratia'') and the numerical organization of territory. These are also features of the wider [[Adriatic Sea|Adriatic]] region, especially [[Etruria]], [[Messapii|Messapia]] and southern Italy.<ref>M. Zaninović, On some relations between Anatolia and Dalmatia, Proceedings of the Xth International Congress of Classical Studies, Ankara-Izmir, 20-30, Sept. 1973, Ankara 1978, 81-93</ref> Toponymical and onomastic connections to Asia Minor may also indicate a Liburnian presence amongst the [[Sea Peoples]].{{sfn|Zaninović|1988}}

The old toponym ''Liburnum'' in [[Liguria]] may also link the Liburnian name to the [[Etruscan civilization|Etruscans]],<ref>M. Fluss, Liburni, PWRE. Bd. V, 583</ref><ref>M. Jokl in Ebert, Reallex. der Vorgeschichte, VI, 46-47{{Full citation needed|date=February 2025}}</ref> as well as the proposed [[Tyrsenian language]] family.

The Liburnians underwent [[Romanization]] after being conquered by the Romans in 35 BCE. The Liburnian language was replaced by [[Latin]] and underwent [[language death]] –most likely during [[Late Antiquity]]. The Liburnians nevertheless retained some of their cultural traditions until the 4th century CE, especially in the larger cities – a fact attested by archaeology.{{sfn|Zaninović|1988}}

==Onomastics==

===Anthroponyms===
{{see also|Proposed Illyrian vocabulary#Proposed Illyrian anthroponyms}}
The single name plus [[patronym]]ic formula common among Illyrians is rare among Liburnians. In a region where the Roman three-name formula (''[[praenomen]]'', ''[[nomen gentile]]'', ''[[cognomen]]'': ''Caius Julius Caesar'') spread at an early date, a native two-name formula appears in several variants.{{sfn|Wilkes|1995|p=78}}
Personal name plus family name is found in southern Liburnia, while personal name plus family name plus patronymic is found throughout the Liburnian area, for example: {{lang|la|Avita Suioca Vesclevesis}}, {{lang|la|Velsouna Suioca Vesclevesis f(ilia)}}, {{lang|la|Avita Aquillia L(uci) f(ilia)}}, {{lang|la|Volsouna Oplica Pl(a)etoris f(ilia)}}, {{lang|la|Vendo Verica Triti f(ilius)}}.{{sfn|Wilkes|1995|p=78}}

[[Image:Iron Age Italy.svg|thumb|upright=1.4|Ethnolinguistic map of Italy in the [[Iron Age]], before the [[Roman conquest of Italy|Roman expansion and conquest of Italy]]]]

Among the personal names of the so-called 'Liburnian' area are Aetor, Ceunus, Cliticus, Curticus, Dmocus, Lambicus, Oplus, Raecus, Suioca, Turus, Vadica, Verica, Viniocus, Volso, Voltimesis, Voltissa, and Zupricus.{{sfn|Neumann|2008|p=396}}

===Theonyms===
{{see also|Proposed Illyrian vocabulary#Illyrian theonyms}}

Among the theonyms of the so-called 'Liburnian' area are female deities Iutossica, Latra and Sentona.{{sfn|Neumann|2008|p=396}} 

* Anzotica or Ansotica - the Liburnian [[Venus (mythology)|Venus]]; worshipped in [[Nin, Croatia|Aenona]].{{sfn|Kurilić|2021|p=141, 151}}
* Iicus - the only male Liburnian deity; worshipped in Aenona.{{sfn|Kurilić|2021|p=141}}
* Iutossica - goddess worshipped in Albona.{{sfn|Kurilić|2021|p=141}}
* Aitica - goddess worshipped in Albona.{{sfn|Kurilić|2021|p=141}}
* Sentona - goddess worshipped in [[Albona]], [[Flanona]] and [[Tarsatica]], among the Northern Liburni.{{sfn|Kurilić|2021|p=142}}
* Latra - goddess worshipped in Nedinum, Corinium, Asseria and Scardona.{{sfn|Kurilić|2021|p=142}}

===Toponyms===
Among the toponyms of the so-called 'Liburnian' area are Aenona, Alvona, Flanona, Fulfinium, Lopsica, Ludrum, and Scardona.{{sfn|Neumann|2008|p=396}}
